item.title: Leiden bars extreme right student group from recruitment events
item.description:
Leiden bars extreme right student group from recruitment events

November 12, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Leiden University has banned the extreme right-wing student association GNSV from advertising club membership to new students during introduction weeks, following years of complaints and an investigation by the national security services.

The intelligence security body AIVD released a report detailing how the group hides behind moderate rhetoric to draw students in, while spreading far-right political agendas privately. Some members have been inspired to plot terror attacks.

Last year, one of its members was arrested for possession of firearms after a raid on his home in Erp in Bradant. The police were tipped off that he was planning a terror attack.

The GNSV, or Greater Netherlands Student Association, is known for spreading conspiracy theories like the Great Replacement, and advocating for remigration. The security services’ report said its members privately hold “deeply racist” views.

Dutch News spoke to its members at Leiden in 2024, where one of the group’s members discussed the idea that Flanders and the Netherlands should reunite and that too many immigrants were coming to the country.

The ban will take effect from next summer, the Volkskrant reported on Thursday. It follows three years of protests against the group’s presence at the event, which is aimed at new students.

“We do not want to offer space for that at our introduction market,” Leiden’s rector magnificus, Sarah de Rijcke, wrote on the university website.

Radboud University in Nijmegen barred the GNSV from its own introduction market immediately after the report came out. In Leiden, eight local council parties asked questions about the university’s policy.

item.title: Cabinet collapse looms as VVD pledges to vote against tax plan
item.description:
Cabinet collapse looms as VVD pledges to vote against tax plan

November 12, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The right-wing liberal VVD will vote against its own cabinet’s tax plan if its coalition partners help pass an opposition amendment raising taxes on the very wealthy, the party’s parliamentary leader said on Thursday.

Ruben Brekelmans told MPs during a reopened debate on the 2027 tax plan that the VVD would not back the bill if the amendment, drawn up by left-wing Pro and pan-European progressive party Volt and supported by centrist D66 and the Christian Democrat CDA, is adopted, broadcaster NOS reported.

Brekelmans repeated party leader Dilan Yesilgöz’s call for a “fundamental reset” of the cabinet and said he had also been caught off guard by the deal. Yesilgöz, who is also defence minister, said on Wednesday evening that it breached the coalition agreement.

Several MPs, including anti-immigration PVV leader Geert Wilders, asked how the VVD could vote against the tax plan while staying in government. Brekelmans declined to say what would happen next. “I’m not going to speculate about what-if questions,” he said.

Earlier in the debate, Wilders accused D66 and the CDA of stabbing the VVD in the back. D66 parliamentary leader Jan Paternotte dismissed this as nonsense.

The amendment introduces a new top rate of 38.5% on returns above €60,000 on box 3 taxes, the levy on savings and investments, while the basic rate falls from 36% to 35.5%. The €1 billion raised will go towards cutting the lowest rate of income tax.

It is not certain the amendment will pass. Christian-social ChristenUnie and pensioners’ party 50PLUS, which had conditionally backed the tax plan, have doubts about how the package is funded.

Only €588 million of the €1 billion is linked to specific measures. The remaining €412 million is a target to be met by tackling tax constructions used by the wealthy. Pro and Volt have suggested an “exit tax” on millionaires who leave the country, to prevent capital flight.

The ChristenUnie and 50PLUS haven’t yet said how they will vote. If they oppose the amendment, it may fail, leaving D66 and the CDA without the senate majority they need. According to NOS, the VVD is urging the ChristenUnie to vote against, while Pro leader Jesse Klaver is trying to win over its leader, Mirjam Bikker.

The three parties in Jetten’s minority cabinet have 66 of the 150 seats in parliament, 10 short of a majority, so they rely on opposition parties to pass legislation.

Economic impact 

Employers’ organisations VNO-NCW and MKB-Nederland said the country could not afford a political crisis, and objected to businesses potentially footing the bill.

But ING chief economist Marieke Blom told NOS the amendment would have very little effect on the Dutch economy, and said she did not expect millionaires or companies to leave the Netherlands because of it. “A cabinet collapse would create new political uncertainty, and I’m worried that we would grind to a halt,” she said.

Prime Minister Rob Jetten said “yes” when asked on arrival whether things would work out. Votes on the amendments and the full tax plan are due after the debate.

If the cabinet does fall, an early general election could be held alongside the provincial and water board elections on March 17 next year, NOS reported. It would be the second cabinet in a row to fall within a year.

item.title: Rozendaal council to dissolve after 200 years of independence
item.description:
Rozendaal council to dissolve after 200 years of independence

November 12, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

After 200 years as an independent council, Rozendaal is seeking to merge with the neighbouring Gelderland councils of Rheden and Brummen, bringing its free-standing era to an end.

The smallest council on the Dutch mainland has some 1,800 residents, and Rozendaal’s council say its independence is no longer viable both financially and organisationally.

“Continuing independently would require significant, ongoing investments in personnel, expertise and systems,” mayor Ingrid Timmer told broadcaster NOS. “We simply do not have the financial capacity for that.”

A merger appeared to be the next best option, and Rheden and Brummen were chosen as both councils are currently going through their own reorganisation process and have close ties to Rozendaal.

The mayor thinks that by merging with them sooner rather than later, Rozendaal can have equal input into the new council, although the other two councils still have to approve that.

Rozendaal Blijft

Some Rozendaal residents are dissenting, saying they feel the process is moving too quickly. They’ve launched a petition with 500 signatures so far asking the council to reconsider.

The local initiative Rozendaal Blijft – Rozendaal Stays – argues that there’s not a compelling, substantiated reason for the council to disband.

“There is no clear indication as to why a decision must be made today, rather than in a few months’ time,” said the group.

“Difficult yet responsible” choice

“The steps we have taken were consistently driven by new insights,” responded mayor Timmer, who acknowledges this was not the outcome officials had hoped for. “As early as the first phase, it became clear that we needed to look beyond the option of continuing as an independent municipality.”

Rheden and Brummen are expected to decide by the end of the year if Rozendaal will join them. Then comes the so-called Reclassification Design, with all three councils deciding, among other things, on the design and name of the new council, its services and finances.

Residents will have an opportunity to respond to the plan, with the aim of forming the new council on January 1, 2030. Early council elections are slated for November 2029.

item.title: Nearly 1 million households face higher mortgages: DNB
item.description:
Nearly 1 million households face higher mortgages: DNB

November 12, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Some 950,000 Dutch households will pay more for their mortgage in the next two years when their fixed interest rate runs out, the central bank DNB said on Thursday.

For the typical household, the monthly bill will go up by around €150 before tax relief. A quarter of the group will pay less than €50 extra, but for another quarter the rise will top €300.

Most Dutch homeowners fix their rate for at least 10 years, and many signed up when rates were at record lows. Five years ago the average rate on a new mortgage was 1.6%, now it is close to 4%.

DNB’s figures cover people with a variable rate or a fixed rate that ends before the end of 2028. They account for 19% of the mortgage debt held by banks.

The central bank said most of them should be able to cope, because wages have gone up sharply in recent years and mortgages are smaller compared with incomes and house values. The typical household will spend 24% of its net income on the mortgage, up from 20%.

But the number of households spending more than 40% of their income on their mortgage is expected to double to around 60,000. The OECD and the ECB see 40% as a sign that a household could run into financial trouble.

People who face a big rise in payments just as their income drops, because they lose their job or retire, are most at risk, DNB said.

More people will be hit after 2028. The rate on another 27% of bank mortgage debt is due to reset between 2029 and 2033.

item.title: Frisian gold coin from 16th century breaks record at auction
item.description:
Frisian gold coin from 16th century breaks record at auction

November 12, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A Frisian gold coin dating back to the Eighty Years’ War has raised a record amount at auction.

The rare gold half Philipsdaalder from 1580 sold for a whopping €369,000 on Wednesday at Heritage Auctions Europe in IJsselstein. It set a record for the most expensive Dutch provincial coin.

The coin features an image of Philip II, the king of Spain and ruler of the Spanish Netherlands at the beginning of the Eighty Years’ War, which broke out in 1568. Despite the revolt, his image still appeared on coins in the early years of the war, hence the coin’s name.

Half Philipsdaalders were minted only in small numbers in Friesland, and just two silver examples from the province are known to exist. The gold coin was last on display in Leeuwarden in 1877, when it belonged to former mayor Rengers.

The auction house hasn’t said who its new owner is.

According to Jacco Scheper of Heritage Auctions Europe, reports AD, the coin fits into a broader trend of exceptional and rare pieces fetching record amounts, whether they be coins or rare Pokémon cards and retro video games.

item.title: Business bankruptcies up 27% on a year earlier in October
item.description:
Business bankruptcies up 27% on a year earlier in October

November 12, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The number of companies declared bankrupt in the Netherlands rose by 27% in October compared with a year earlier, according to figures from national statistics office CBS.

A total of 322 businesses went bankrupt last month, 69 more than in October 2025 and one more than in September, the CBS said on Thursday.

It is the third month in a row in which bankruptcies have been higher than in the same month a year earlier. Before that, they had fallen year on year in six of the first seven months of 2026.

The bankruptcy rate rose to 8.5 per 100,000 businesses, from 6.8 in October last year. That is still below the levels of 2024, when the rate peaked at 11.3 in July. The CBS said the rate has fluctuated between seven and eight since the middle of 2025.

Hospitality had the highest bankruptcy rate in October, at 25.1 per 100,000 businesses, up from 23.3 a year earlier. Industry saw the biggest increase, from 19.5 to 24.8. Construction was one of the few sectors where the rate fell, from 14 to 12.5.

The number of company failures fell by 15% across 2025 as a whole.

item.title: Minister: goal for zero homelessness by 2030 scrapped
item.description:
Minister: goal for zero homelessness by 2030 scrapped

November 12, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Long-term care minister Mirjam Sterk told parliament on Wednesday that the government’s goal to reduce homelessness to zero by 2030 is impossible, saying she wanted to “tell the honest story”.

The fourth Rutte cabinet set that goal in 2022 in its National Action Plan for Homelessness, seeking to move away from temporary emergency shelters towards permanent housing, backed by a €450 million annual budget.

“We remain committed, but it’s incredibly tough,” said the minister, who had informed parliament of her intentions in a letter last week. The announcement took some MPs by surprise.

“I did expect some urgency from this cabinet, but what I see is indifference,” socialist party SP MP Sandra Beckerman said.

And while the government says it will do its best to bring down the rising numbers of homeless people via existing plans to arrange suitable housing, parliament members from Pro, the ChristenUnie, D66 and CDA remain unconvinced.

The mayors

In response, the mayors of the four major Dutch cities wrote a letter to the House of Representatives on behalf of 40 other large councils asking for an additional €100 million to provide more emergency shelters and help treat crack and cocaine addicts, among other things.

Alderman Arjen Dubbelaar of The Hague says he needs €14 million to offer shelter to homeless people. “That deficit is only increasing,” he said. “We don’t want people to sleep in parks, but at the same time our reception locations are packed.”

The minister says that money won’t be forthcoming until the Chamber first figures out where the current allocation is being spent, and no new targets have been set.

Some 33,000 people aged between 18 and 65 in the Netherlands currently have no permanent place to live, most of them in the big cities, where it is relatively easy to earn money. The real figure may be higher, as it is not known how many people are staying with family or friends.

item.title: “Dutch directness was a relief, and a kind of healing”
item.description:
“Dutch directness was a relief, and a kind of healing”

November 12, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Elena Melkumova was head of education at a contemporary art museum in Moscow when a 2016 conference trip persuaded her to study museology in Amsterdam. She came back in 2022 and, after three years in the lighting industry, now creates educational programmes for lighting designers while working as an independent curator. She finds Dutch directness a relief and recommends a 12km walk through the dunes to the sea.

How did you end up in the Netherlands?
In 2016 I was head of education at Garage Museum of Contemporary Art in Moscow, and I was invited to an International Council of Museums conference on exchange between Dutch and Russian museum professionals. I fell for the country almost immediately: the professional community, the way people talked about culture, the networking. After the first day of the conference I called my mother and told her I wanted to study here.

So I ended up doing my master’s degree in museology at the Reinwardt Academie of the AHK. It was quite a spontaneous move. In 2022 I came back to Amsterdam, without any proper plan, because of the geopolitical situation. Since then my path has taken an unexpected turn. For three years I left museums for the lighting industry, but now I am slowly but surely coming back to the cultural field.

Today I combine the two worlds: I create educational programmes for lighting designers, and as an independent curator I still make exhibitions, most recently at the National Gallery of Armenia, with a Dutch artist among the participants. I hope to bring this exhibition to the Netherlands soon as well.

How do you describe yourself: expat, lovepat, immigrant, international?
In 2016 I felt 100% international, as I came because I had fallen in love with a professional culture. When I moved in 2022, I felt more like an immigrant at first, as I was genuinely puzzled about what to do and how to define myself. Now I feel international again. My work has always moved between countries, and that in-between position is where I am most at home.

How long do you plan to stay?
Each winter I have a different answer to that. Maybe I need to plan more of my holidays for the winter, and that will change. Last year I spent the winter in Portugal, and it was amazing. But coming back to the question: if I am honest, I have stopped answering that with a number. The Netherlands has shaped how I work and who I am now, and that stays with me wherever I am.

Do you speak Dutch and how did you learn?
By now my Dutch is good enough to follow work meetings, but not good enough to stop everyone at the bakery from switching to English. Strangely, the more I understand, the higher the barrier to speaking seems to get. I just need to push through it. Combining serious study with a full-time job and freelance work has been a challenge, but I have promised myself that next year I will get serious about learning and practising.

What’s your favourite Dutch thing?
Directness. I come from a culture where reading between the lines is perhaps too common a skill. In a Dutch workplace, when your manager says something, that is what they mean, and you do not have to spend the evening decoding it. For me that was a relief, and honestly a kind of healing.

How Dutch have you become?
I think I have become more direct and much more functional. I now judge things, from a bicycle to an exhibition layout, first by whether they work.

Which three Dutch people (dead or alive) would you most like to meet?
Bas Jan Ader, the conceptual artist who vanished at sea in 1975 while attempting to cross the Atlantic in a tiny boat, as part of his work In Search of the Miraculous. I would like to ask him what he was looking for.

Karel Martens, who makes his prints with found objects on an old letterpress. I would like to know how he has kept playing for sixty years.

And Robby Müller, the cinematographer who often worked only with natural or found light. I would like to ask him what he looked for first when he walked into a room.

What’s your top tourist tip?
Take a train, leave the city and get lost in the dunes somewhere by the sea. My favourite long walk: take the train to Overveen and cross the dunes to the Parnassia aan Zee beach pavillion, looking out for all the animals on the way. Stop there for a soda or an ice cream and maybe a dip in the sea, then walk on to Bloemendaal aan Zee and have mussels for lunch at one of the lovely beach bars with a view.

Then slowly but surely carry on to Zandvoort aan Zee and take the train back to the city. It is an easy 12 km walk. But if the weather is not great (so, half of the year, haha), I would recommend spending half a day at the Eye Filmmuseum: first see the current temporary exhibition, then have a quick lunch at the café overlooking the IJ, and finally watch one of the classics on 35mm.

Tell us something surprising you’ve found out about the Netherlands.
I was stunned at the beginning, and I am still amazed by how physically active people are here. People in this country spend so much time outside cycling, walking, exercising and even swimming, and I have adopted that 100%.

If you had just 24 hours left in the Netherlands, what would you do?
I would take my dog for a long early-morning walk in the Amsterdamse Bos. Then I would pay a short visit to the Stedelijk or the Rijksmuseum to see a few of my favourite pieces. After that I would have lunch with friends somewhere on a terrace.

Then I would take a train to the sea for a relaxed walk in the dunes and eat some oysters on the beach. Back in the city, I would use my Cineville card in the evening to see a great film at a cosy neighbourhood cinema, preferably LAB111 in Amsterdam, my all-time favourite.

Elena was talking with Louis Gore-Langton

item.title: Coalition on knife edge as VVD weighs response to tax deal
item.description:
Coalition on knife edge as VVD weighs response to tax deal

November 12, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The future of the coalition government is hanging by a thread after ruling parties centrist D66 and the Christian Democrat CDA struck a tax deal with two opposition parties on Wednesday, despite staunch objections from their coalition partner, the right-wing liberal VVD.

VVD leader Dilan Yesilgöz told reporters on Wednesday evening that the deal breached the coalition agreement, and that she wanted talks on a “fundamental reset” if D66 and the CDA went ahead with it.

According to broadcaster NOS, D66 and the CDA will vote for the amendment agreed with left-wing Pro and pro-European party Volt, regardless of what the VVD decides. The amendment will raise taxes on the very wealthy to cut the lowest rate of income tax.

The VVD had said it was “unthinkable” it could vote for the amendment in its original form, with MP Wendy van Eijk calling it “bad for the Netherlands”.

Yesilgöz said the new, watered-down version was still “a bad deal”, and that the VVD had been “caught off guard”. “Of course, if D66 and CDA would rather have a coalition agreement with Pro, then just say it,” she said.

Prime Minister Rob Jetten pulled out of an EU meeting in Dublin to attend Thursday’s debate on the tax plan, which starts at 10.15am Thursday.

The amendment D66 and the CDA agreed with Pro and Volt is a watered-down version of a “millionaires’ tax”. It would raise €1 billion, down from €1.5 billion in Pro and Volt’s original plan. It adds a new top rate of 38.5% in box 3, the tax on savings and investments. The money will go towards cutting the lowest rate of income tax.

Pro leader Jesse Klaver said the VVD was not involved in the negotiations. CDA leader Henri Bontenbal said the VVD had been kept informed “at several moments”.

Parliament backed a motion on Tuesday saying that if a cabinet collapses mid-term, MPs should first discuss forming a new coalition before new elections are called. Only one Dutch cabinet since 2000 has survived its full four-year term.

item.title: D66 and CDA agree deal with Pro to save budget, VVD frozen out
item.description:
D66 and CDA agree deal with Pro to save budget, VVD frozen out

November 11, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Coalition parties D66 and CDA have agreed an eleventh-hour deal with the left-wing Pro to break the deadlock in the Dutch budget talks.

The opposition party announced an amendment to raise an extra €1 billion in taxes on assets and savings, shortly after a 2pm deadline for changes to the cabinet’s tax plan expired.

The third party in the minority government, the right-wing liberal VVD, is expected to vote against the amendment, but enough minor parties are likely to support it to ensure a majority in the Lower House.

Prime minister Rob Jetten has cancelled a trip to Dublin for an EU leaders’ summit so he can attend an extra debate on the budget scheduled for Thursday morning.

The VVD has not responded to the announcement on the deal, but will now have to decided whether to accept the amended budget or withdraw its support altogether, which would trigger a cabinet collapse.

The amendment is a watered-down version of the original plan, tabled by Pro and pro-European party Volt, to raise an extra €1.5 billion by creating a new top tax rate for savers and investors with assets of more than €1.3 million. D66 and CDA described that proposal as “too coarse”.

The updated version will also bring an increase in tax on inheritance and cash gifts, and a pledge to crack down on tax avoidance schemes.

Millionaires’ tax

“This is a breakthrough,” said Pro party leader Jesse Klaver. “In the last few days we have held talks to bring about a compromise to make the Netherlands fairer. If this plan is accepted, the Netherlands will have a millionaires’ tax.”

The VVD was not involved in the negotiations, Klaver added. “We have talked to D66 and CDA. If you want to know if the VVD support it, you’ll have to ask them.”

Earlier the VVD said it was “unthinkable” it could vote for the amendment in its original form, with MP Wendy van Eijk saying the plan crossed her party’s “pain threshold” and was “bad for the Netherlands”.

Now the deadline to submit amendments has passed, the VVD will have to decide whether it can still support the budget with the wealth tax included. If not, it will mean the end of the coalition.

On Tuesday parliament voted for a motion calling on the cabinet to explore alternative coalitions before it decides to call early elections, in an attempt to prevent the third general election in just over three years.

If an election is called, it is expected to take place in March. In the meantime a caretaker government would have to try to cobble together a majority in parliament for a new budget plan.
